author: Rudyard Kipling
poem_text_en:
We were taken from the ore-bed and the mine,
We were melted in the furnace and the pit 
We were cast and wrought and hammered to design,
We were cut and filed and tooled and gauged to fit.
Some water, coal, and oil is all we ask,
And a thousandth of an inch to give us play:
And now, if you will set us to our task,
We will serve you four and twenty hours a day!
We can pull and haul and push and lift and drive,
We can print and plough and weave and heat and light,
We can run and race and swim and fly and dive,
We can see and hear and count and read and write!
But remember, please, the Law by which we live,
We are not built to comprehend a lie,
We can neither love nor pity nor forgive,
 If you make a slip in handling us you die!
Though our smoke may hide the Heavens from your eyes,
It will vanish and the stars will shine again,
Because, for all our power and weight and size,
We are nothing more than children of your brain!
summary_en: The poem explores the power of modern machines, describing how they are created from raw materials to serve humanity's needs tirelessly. While machines possess immense capability, the poem concludes by reminding the reader that they are ultimately products of the human intellect and lack human emotion or moral judgment. It highlights the potential danger to humans if they mishandle these powerful inventions.

rules.rule_en: Rudyard Kipling was born on December 30, 1865, in Bombay, India.
Rudyard Kipling received the 1907 Nobel Prize in Literature.
The rhyme scheme of the final stanza is a,b,a,b.
The 'Law' of the machines is that they are not built to understand lies and cannot love, pity, or forgive.

worked_exercises.prompt_en: Who does ‘we’ refer to in first stanza?
‘And a thousandth of an inch to give us play:’ Which of the following do the machines want to prove from this line?
worked_exercises.answer_en: Once Machines are fed with fuel, they start quickly.
